title: pregnancy in effectiveness trials of hiv prevention agents
display_name: Pregnancy in Effectiveness Trials of HIV Prevention Agents
abstract: despite remarkable progress over the past several decades in understanding the biology and epidemiology of the hiv pandemic, the virus continues to spread relentlessly. diverse prevention approaches are desperately needed to reverse this trend. for many women, products that can be used without the cooperation of male partners are critical. multiple such products are currently being tested in large-scale effectiveness trials, and many more are in earlier stages of development. these products include physical and chemical barriers to viral entry, vaginal ph buffers, an antiherpes drug, antiretroviral drugs, and other agents. some of these products may have contraceptive as well as anti-infective activity.1 the basic design of hiv prevention trials is standard: hiv-negative women at risk for hiv infection are randomly assigned to use either the study product or a placebo according to a specified schedule (e.g., daily or before each coital act) and then are followed to assess hiv incidence. most hiv prevention trials are conducted in resource-poor settings in africa and asia where hiv incidence is high. to reach the required study population, these trials must enroll sexually active women of reproductive age. most of these women will be at risk for pregnancy as well as hiv infection. early studies evaluating the hiv prevention effectiveness of the spermicidal compound nonoxynol-9 reported few pregnancies.2 8 in contrast, some ongoing trials of candidate microbicides and oral antiviral agents are finding pregnancy rates between 16 and 64 per 100 woman-years.9 12 the difference between earlier and recent findings is due in part to the different approaches used to ascertain pregnancies in these studies. high pregnancy rates have major implications for the conduct and interpretation of hiv prevention trials. in november 2005, family health international hosted a meeting of hiv prevention researchers and selected experts to discuss the range of issues related to this topic. in this article, we summarize the important themes covered at that and subsequent meetings and provide a comprehensive discussion of the complexities of the topic to help guide the multidisciplinary field. we do not offer prescriptive recommendations but instead hope to assist investigators in making appropriate decisions about how best to design their individual trials. ensuring safety in hiv prevention effectiveness trials the welfare of study participants is a paramount concern in all clinical research. most of the hiv prevention agents and all of the candidate vaginal microbicides under development are investigational products; little or no human data exist regarding their safety in pregnancy. although some of these products are not systemically absorbed through the skin or genital mucosa, an embryo or fetus may be exposed by direct passage of the product through the cervical canal and into the uterus, and sperm are exposed during intercourse. high pregnancy rates in trials of these products accentuate the importance of establishing safeguards to protect pregnant women and their babies from any harmful effects that might occur. perspectives differ on the best way to optimize safety. the cautious view that is conventional in drug development research has been the stance adopted thus far in hiv prevention research. this view holds that if clinically important harm from product use during pregnancy cannot be positively ruled out, trials should be designed to prevent exposure of pregnant women to the product. in theory, exposure could be prevented either by precluding pregnancy among participants or by prohibiting product use once pregnancy occurs. most recent and ongoing hiv prevention trial protocols emphasize the latter strategy. however, strict implementation of this strategy is unachievable, because pregnancies are not identifiable as soon as they occur. even sensitive pregnancy tests cannot reliably detect the pregnancy hormone human chorionic gonadotropin (hcg) earlier than several weeks after fertilization.13,14 because trials can perform pregnancy tests only intermittently, some pregnancies may remain unrecognized for weeks to months after conception. therefore, a policy of stopping product use only after a pregnancy is identified will frequently fail to eliminate exposure during very early gestation. because gestational weeks 2 to 6 after fertilization are the period of greatest vulnerability to most serious toxic insults,15 this strategy can provide only partial protection from potential adverse effects of the hiv prevention. furthermore, the concern has been raised that this strategy could potentially lead some trial participants who become pregnant to have induced abortions so that they can resume product use. such a consequence would be particularly undesirable in settings where abortion is illegal or unsafe. to our knowledge, this theoretical concern has not been documented in any ongoing hiv prevention trial. nevertheless, both to minimize any effects of product exposure in early pregnancy and to minimize potential ethical concerns about encouraging abortion, the best primary approach is to prevent unintended pregnancies from occurring in the first place. indeed, united states food and drug administration regulations strongly recommend that female trial participants be required to use effective contraceptives in trials if the safety of the study product in pregnancy has not been established. the alternative position maintains that if sufficient preclinical data and other evidence contain no indication that a product is harmful to a pregnant woman or a developing embryo, informed trial participants should be allowed to make their own decisions about using it during pregnancy. this approach might be quite reasonable, for example, if appropriate preclinical studies found no evidence of adverse effects on embryonic, fetal, or postnatal development in animals, genotoxicity studies found no evidence of mutagenic potential, and available data showed no sign that the product is carcinogenic. the opportunity provided by this approach to collect information on the safety of the product in pregnancy would be valuable, because these products will certainly be used by pregnant women once they are marketed. in addition, this approach is consistent with the ethical principle of autonomy, and it may have particular interest for women who intend not to carry a pregnancy to term. the quantity and types of evidence that would be required to justify allowing product use during pregnancy and the specific information to be provided to participants would have to be decided for each individual trial after consultation with regulatory agencies, ethics boards, and other experts. preclinical reproductive toxicity studies can be expensive and lengthy, but this cost may be justified in view of the potential benefits of this approach. interpretation of trial data high pregnancy rates in hiv prevention trials pose several concerns for the interpretation of data. first, if participants reduce their use of the study product during pregnancy (either in compliance with a trial requirement or on their own initiative) then the maximum detectable effectiveness of the product is reduced, as is the power to detect this lower effectiveness level. the impact could be quite substantial. for example, consider a trial of a coital-dependent product designed to have 80% power to detect a 50% reduction in hiv incidence in a population of women who, on average, use the product for 80% of coital acts over 1 year of follow-up. if an additional 10% of acts that would otherwise have been protected are without product due to pregnancy (e.g., 40% of women become pregnant, and each pregnancy lasts 3 months) then the total amount of time off product would be 28%, not 20%. this seemingly modest reduction in product use will reduce the observable effectiveness to 45%, and it will dramatically increase by one-third the number of hiv infections required to achieve 80% power in an intent-to-treat analysis (table 1). increasing the study size to enroll this many additional women would be a large undertaking.table 1: effect of product nonuse on power and study sizea second analytic problem could arise if the experimental and placebo groups have different pregnancy rates, as might occur, for example, if the study product is contraceptive. some evidence suggests that hiv risk may be altered during pregnancy, either because of biologic changes that affect the likelihood of transmission or changes in sexual practices or other behaviors.16 thus, any observed effect of a candidate agent on hiv incidence could result from a combination of its direct hiv prevention activity and its indirect impact on changes in hiv risk associated with pregnancy. presumably both the underlying pregnancy rate and the contraceptive effectiveness of the study product would have to be large for such changes to bias substantially the estimates of treatment effects. in the extreme case, however, a trial of a product that is highly contraceptive but has no direct anti-hiv activity could yield results apparently consistent with effectiveness (e.g., if hiv risk increases disproportionately in the placebo arm due to a higher pregnancy rate). an opposite result could occur if pregnancy is associated with decreased hiv risk: an efficacious product that is also contraceptive could falsely appear to be ineffective. the mechanisms in such cases could be difficult or impossible to sort out using trial data. unlike the power issue discussed previously, this problem could arise regardless of whether product use is suspended during pregnancy. preventing pregnancy in trials the optimal way both to allay safety concerns and to ensure analytic validity of hiv prevention trials is to minimize the number of pregnancies. many trials currently exclude women who express an active desire for pregnancy within the follow-up period. strengthening this criterion in specific ways (for example, by more intensive questioning or by excluding women who may desire pregnancy shortly after completing the trial) might increase its effectiveness. ultimately, though, in young, sexually active populations, minimization of pregnancy rates requires widespread practice of effective contraception. the most effective contraceptive methods are intrauterine devices, hormone implants, hormone injections, and sterilization (table 2). risk of pregnancy among typical users of these methods is 3% or less in the first year.17 oral contraceptive pills and other short-term hormonal methods (patch, ring) are much less effective in many populations, primarily because inconsistent use is common. for example, in the united states, almost half of low-income, cohabiting (not married) women who are younger than 20 years become pregnant in the first year of use of oral contraceptive pills.18 the potential utility of these short-term methods for reducing pregnancy rates in trial populations may therefore be limited. male condoms and other barrier methods are not effective enough as sole contraceptive methods in young women with high coital frequency to assure low pregnancy rates in trials, although of course male condoms are recommended to all trial participants for protection from infections.table 2: attributes of contraceptive methodsdespite the obvious benefits, increasing effective contraceptive use within hiv prevention trials may be problematic. in many settings where trials are conducted, a full range of contraceptive services may not be available. in addition, women's ability to access services that do exist may be limited by cost, misunderstandings about the methods, lack of transportation to the dispensing site, overly restrictive eligibility requirements, substandard quality of care, and other barriers. therefore, to increase contraception use in a trial may require the development of a new or revised family planning infrastructure, either as part of the trial organization or in collaboration with a separate local facility. such an undertaking could have considerable implications for the complexity of the trial, the workload of the study staff, and the study budget. the sustainability of this infrastructure after the trial is concluded also needs to be factored in; abrupt withdrawal of such services may cause problems for individual trial participants who may need specific method-related follow-up such as iud or implant removal, for the larger community, and for future research in that community and elsewhere. given the importance of lowering pregnancy rates in trials, though, finding ways to resolve these concerns may be worth the cost. for example, one option would be to place trials selectively in locations where contraceptives are already available, affordable, and widely used. many women would undoubtedly consider access to contraceptive services to be a welcome benefit of trial participation. but at some sites, a substantial segment of the population may be reluctant to use these services because of fear of method side effects, stigma, or confusion about a requirement for "triple protection" (the study product, condoms, and the contraceptive). under such conditions, the only way to ensure low pregnancy rates is to restrict enrollment to women who agree in advance to use one of a specified set of methods for the duration of their expected participation in the trial. if this approach is adopted, contraceptive use should be carefully monitored throughout the trial so that participants who are not using their method consistently can be appropriately counseled. if the hiv prevention product is considered unsafe in pregnancy, this counseling should include an instruction to suspend its use until effective contraception is resumed. however, these measures might affect many aspects of the study: recruitment, the characteristics of the study population, retention, adherence with use of the study product, and sexual behavior patterns. in addition, extensive practice of contraception in trials may affect trial outcomes. for example, hormonal contraceptives may alter the susceptibility of the vaginal and cervical mucosa to local effects of the study product, which could complicate assessment of safety. because these methods may cause changes in vaginal bleeding patterns, they may obviate the utility of abnormal vaginal bleeding as a sign of potential reproductive tract toxicity. presumably, because effectiveness trials are randomized and masked, these effects should be equally distributed between groups and therefore should not compromise internal trial validity. however, any interactions between contraceptives and hiv prevention products could affect the power of the study to detect differences in safety outcomes between groups as well as the external generalizability of the study results. identification and care of pregnant women ascertainment of pregnancies in trials is essential to inform the analysis of effectiveness, to allow collection of data about product safety during pregnancy, and to trigger counseling of pregnant women about continuation of product use. if the safety of product use during pregnancy is an important concern, pregnancies should be detected as early in gestation as possible. regularly scheduled, frequent urine pregnancy testing, as in current trials, is expedient for this purpose. researchers should be aware, however, that many modern pregnancy tests are so sensitive that they may detect subclinical pregnancies that would not otherwise have been recognized either by women or providers. more frequent use of these tests thus will increase the total number of pregnancies ascertained, which, as noted above, will reduce the ability of the trial to show efficacy of the study product if women are required to stop product use during pregnancy. in addition, care must be taken to avert misunderstandings of the significance of subclinical pregnancies. women who do not want to be mothers should be discouraged from needlessly seeking induced abortion to terminate these naturally self-limited pregnancies; specifically, they should be advised not to take such action until a pregnancy is confirmed by clinical signs (e.g., missed menses) or by a second pregnancy test. furthermore, participants and the wider community may need explicit education to preclude or correct the mistaken impression that the study product or the trial is either directly or indirectly causing women to become pregnant or that it is causing an increase in rates of miscarriage or induced abortion. alternative pregnancy ascertainment algorithms, such as schemes based on clinical signs of pregnancy or less frequent pregnancy testing, may reduce detection of subclinical pregnancies but likely at the cost of delaying the diagnosis of some clinical pregnancies. delay in diagnosis would be a problem if minimizing product exposure in early pregnancy to the product is a priority. if the safety of the product in pregnancy is in such doubt that trial participants are prohibited from using it during pregnancy, then the trial may have a responsibility to offer counseling and care to participants who become pregnant, particularly if the trial does not provide effective contraceptives. what specific types of care should be offered in these situations needs further consideration; an example is prenatal care followed by treatment of babies who may have suffered product-related toxicity. the united states government, which supports most of the ongoing trials, currently forbids recipients of federal funds from providing abortion or referrals for abortion and indeed even from mentioning abortion as an option. however, conducting trials of potentially embryotoxic drugs in locations where legal, safe abortion services are not available may be considered ethically inappropriate. if a study product may expose a neonate to a risk of toxicity through breast milk, participants who are breastfeeding should be counseled about the potential risks of using the product. hiv prevention trials should collect specific safety data from women who become pregnant or who are breastfeeding during the trial. at minimum, these data should include information on timing and amount of product use during pregnancy; pregnancy duration, pregnancy outcome (insofar as collection of data does not put the participants or the trial staff in legal jeopardy), abnormalities of fetal growth or development, and maternal health during pregnancy and the immediate postpartum or postabortion period. if the protocol requires that participants suspend product use during pregnancy, it should also specify when they may resume use after the pregnancy. for the assessment of efficacy, minimizing the amount of time off product is desirable. therefore, in the absence of evidence that product use in the postpartum or postabortion period is dangerous for women or their breastfeeding babies, product use should be restarted as soon as possible after the end of each pregnancy. in practice, though, determining that a pregnancy has in fact ended can be challenging. in subclinical pregnancies, hcg elevation is by definition transitory, so a follow-up pregnancy test a week or two after the diagnosis of a very early pregnancy may be a convenient way to trigger prompt resumption of product use after such events. after a clinical pregnancy, in contrast, hcg concentrations decline slowly; pregnancy tests may remain positive for weeks or even months.19 therefore, waiting for a negative pregnancy test may be inefficient. for these pregnancies, alternate indicators that the pregnancy has ended should be considered, such as credible patient history or reliable documentation of abortion or expulsion of products of conception. conclusions management of the many issues related to pregnancy is a substantial challenge for researchers conducting effectiveness trials of hiv prevention agents. strategies designed to address this challenge will have implications for other trial features such as recruitment, retention, cost, and organization. trade-offs inevitably must be made.

title: autonomous driving: a survey of technological gaps using google scholar and web of science trend analysis
display_name: Autonomous Driving: A Survey of Technological Gaps Using Google Scholar and Web of Science Trend Analysis
abstract: autonomous driving (ad) introduces dramatic changes to the way we travel. this emerging technology has the potential to impact the transportation sector across a wide array of categories including safety, efficiency, congestion, legislation, and travel behavior. in this survey, we review the main issues involved in ad as discussed in the literature, and shed light on topics that we consider requiring further development based on google scholar and the web of science (wos) data base. the paper also provides the results of research trends related to autonomous driving based on analysis of the number of search results listed in google trends. according to our research, the fields of vehicle-to-vehicle (v2v) and vehicle-to-cloud (v2c) networking are of higher interest due to the technological gaps and standardization processes. in addition, cyber and security research is in acceleration due to its importance.

title: routing protocols for unmanned aerial vehicle-aided vehicular ad hoc networks: a survey
display_name: Routing Protocols for Unmanned Aerial Vehicle-Aided Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks: A Survey
abstract: in intelligent transportation systems, a vehicular ad hoc network (vanet) has a significant impact in enhancing road safety, traffic management efficiency, and in-vehicle infotainment features. routing in a vanet is hampered by frequent link disconnection for non-line-of-sight communication due to roadside obstacles, high mobility, and frequent topological changes. with the help of three-dimensional movement capability, an unmanned aerial vehicle (uav) can drastically improve the routing experience of a vanet, by increasing the line-of-sight probability, better connectivity, and efficient store-carry-forward mechanism. as a result, various routing protocols with different objectives have been reported for uav-aided vanets. several surveys have been conducted based on different routing protocols for vanets so far. however, to the best of the authors' knowledge, no survey exists till now that dedicatedly covers routing protocols for uav-aided vanets. this survey paper presents a comprehensive review on state-of-the-art routing protocols for uav-aided vanets. the protocols are categorized into seven groups in terms of their working mechanism and design principles. the shortcomings of the protocols are identified individually by critically analyzing them with regard to their advantages, disadvantages, application areas, and future improvements. the routing protocols are qualitatively compared with each other in tabular format as well on the basis of various design aspects and system parameters. in particular, not only performance and special features but also optimization criteria and techniques are extensively discussed in addition to the tabular comparison. furthermore, open research issues and challenges are summarized and discussed.
